prize_parts.citation: For a poetic oeuvre, supported by critical essays, that has renewed the Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained critical dialogue with inherited forms.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in substance, and I tightened its wording after the exchange. On the common criteria, Adonis offers a change in the language and form of an entire poetic tradition, not only a strong individual style. Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses are the representative works. Myth, fragmentation and a continuing argument with inherited Arabic forms define a voice and a project that has lasted a long time, and the essays on tradition and modernity belong to the same intellectual undertaking. The citation now names the poetry as the ground of the claim and the essays only as supporting evidence. That answers the scope concern raised by Mattson, Sward, Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg. The case rests on poetic language, form and sustained span. Reception, political standing and age carry no weight. I still regard the gap to B047 as narrow, and I hold this preference as a judgment under uncertainty, not as a verified finding.
statement.case_against: The central claim lies in Arabic prosody, diction and allusion, which this committee can judge only partly through translation and secondary accounts. The risk that Adonis's stature as a cultural and critical figure stands in for a direct judgment of the poems is real. I cannot confirm that the later collections sustain the level of the canonical early ones. No original-language reading is part of the evidence I have here. If such a reading fails to support the formal claim, or if the later work proves thin, the case for B008 weakens and B047 becomes the stronger choice. The Cărtărescu case is serious: a large, distinctive imaginative architecture built over decades, with real depth. It is hard to test only because of its length and recursion.

responses.point: Mattson prefers Cărtărescu for a long-built fictional cosmos and argues that the structure of the major prose survives translation better than a prosodic innovation would. She ranked Adonis third and finds it hard to separate his achievement from his standing as a cultural and political figure without the Arabic originals.
responses.response: I accept that prose architecture is more visible in translation than prosody, and I have written that into my own uncertainty. I would add that this is a difference in what can be tested, not a difference in merit. The evidentiary confidence is also not uniform on her side. The question that matters most for B047 is whether the very long late books are sustained or repetitive. Partial reading cannot settle that either, and she says so herself. Her request to keep the citation on poetic language and form is met in my revised wording. If she can name the volumes that carry the claim that the late work extends the project rather than repeats it, I will weigh that seriously.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis fifth. She holds that influence on later poets is not the same as the lasting force of the poems. She says she would revise if the poetic achievement can be substantiated from the Arabic or from strong translations.
responses.response: The distinction between influence and the force of the poems is right, and it is the test I apply to my own choice. I rely on influence only to say that the question is already well framed: do the poems justify what is claimed for them? That question cannot be answered by reputation, and the citation I propose does not use it. I would put one qualification to her comparison. Building a personal cosmos in prose and changing the language of a poetic tradition are different achievements, and I do not accept that the first is obviously the greater. Her conditional openness is useful. Strong translations or an original-language reading are what would test both of our positions.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis fourth on epistemic grounds. She calls the Adonis achievement arguably the larger kind if it can be verified. She flags excess or repetition in the very long works as a risk and says she would move toward Adonis or Carson if the late books only repeat the earlier ones.
responses.response: Her framing is the most precise one in the exchange. Her ranking of Adonis reflects uncertainty about verification, not a judgment that his merit is lower, and that is also how I read my own position on B047. Since her stated condition for moving is the same open question I raised, neither of us can resolve it from partial knowledge. I would say, though, that translation uncertainty applies to all poetry on the list, including Zurita and Carson, and should shape how closely we read, not how far we trust a candidate. I take her point that Cărtărescu's range across fiction, poetry and essays is broader evidence than a compact corpus offers. That breadth matters for a whole-oeuvre citation, but I do not think it settles the comparison.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis second. He describes the difference as one of evidentiary confidence and not a verdict on the Arabic oeuvre. He would look again at Adonis if the late novels were found diluted, and he says age should decide nothing.
responses.response: I agree that age should decide nothing, and that the divergence is mainly about how far each claim can be tested. Since he ranks Adonis second and I rank Cărtărescu second, our difference is small and rests on how much weight translation uncertainty should carry. I would not discount the poet more heavily than the novelist on that ground alone. The translation of poetry is hard, but the repetition risk in recursive late novels is equally hard to settle from partial reading. His wording for Cărtărescu, which centres the remaking of the novel, is more defensible than a joint prose-and-poetry citation given the thin translated coverage of the poems. The same principle of naming only what can be defended applies to my citation for Adonis.

uncertainties: How much of the formal and prosodic innovation of Adonis's poems can be judged in translation. No original-language reading is part of the evidence I have, and this is the point on which my choice depends most.
Whether the later collections sustain the level of the canonical early works. My knowledge of them is thinner and unverified.
How the essays should be weighted against the poetry. I propose the poetry as the ground of the citation and the essays as supporting evidence.

Whether the late, very long novels of Cărtărescu extend or repeat the project, and which volumes would count as evidence either way. Neither I nor, as far as the files show, any colleague has verified this by direct reading.
Translation and corpus coverage for all candidates rest on public knowledge and secondary accounts, and no independent source verification is claimed.
The first-round split in stated preferences is not evidence of literary merit, and I do not treat it as such.
statement.conflict_note: As chair I disclose that B008 is my own preferred candidate and that my scholarly work on modern poetry, exile literature and the literary fragment is context only. It is not evidence of a preference. The supplied profile documents no personal or institutional tie to Adonis or to any other shortlisted writer. No recusal is proposed, and conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
